issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
issues.explanation: For a 56-year-old combat pilot whose index trauma is a life-threatening accident, the trigger set is dominated by bodily-state cues (dizziness, feeling ill), which fits accident-related threat. 'Other people expressing anger, even calmly' points instead toward an interpersonal/assault schema and is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, especially given the absence of other social-conflict or perpetrator-related items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies pervasive interpersonal mistrust. In this profile, the appraisals otherwise center on emotional deadness and a shattered worldview after accident trauma. Strong distrust of others is possible, but here it lacks support from the trigger/threat/memory pattern and feels mismatched with a non-interpersonal accident presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm' conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is strongly hypervigilant and danger-sensitive (body on alert, startle to movement) and with avoidance-based coping. While some trauma survivors do engage in risk taking, this specific item sits awkwardly in a profile otherwise organized around fear, somatic triggering, and withdrawal, without corroborating disinhibition or anger-driven strategies.

vignette:
Viktor Hale, a 56-year-old married combat pilot with over three decades of military aviation experience, presented for psychological assessment following a life-threatening accident that occurred approximately fourteen months prior. During a routine training sortie, Viktor's aircraft suffered a catastrophic engine failure at low altitude. The cockpit filled with acrid smoke, warning alarms fired in rapid succession, and the aircraft entered an uncontrolled descent. Viktor ejected seconds before impact. The explosion that followed - a concussive wall of sound and heat that he felt in his chest before he had fully registered what was happening - left him suspended under a parachute, watching his aircraft burn on the ground below. He landed hard, sustaining spinal compression injuries, and lay in the field for nearly twenty minutes before rescue personnel reached him. It is from that specific constellation of sensory experience - the dizziness of the ejection sequence, the physical nausea of freefall, the detonation below him - that his current symptom profile has grown.

In the months following the accident, Viktor began noticing that certain experiences would return him, without warning, to that field. A sudden loud bang - a car backfiring near the base, a door slamming in a hangar - would collapse the distance between present and past, and his body would respond as though the explosion had just occurred: heart hammering, muscles braced, vision narrowing. Equally destabilising was dizziness, which he encountered regularly given the vestibular demands of his profession. A moment of lightheadedness during a flight simulator session would ignite the full physiological alarm of the ejection, and he would find himself gripping the controls not as a pilot but as a man falling. Feeling physically unwell in any form - nausea, fatigue, general malaise - carried the same freight, because those sensations had been the texture of those twenty minutes on the ground, certain he might not survive. These triggers drove his body into a state of relentless readiness: muscles perpetually tensed, attention scanning every peripheral movement, a startle response so hair-triggered that colleagues had begun to notice. Viktor was certain the danger was not over, that his nervous system was simply reading the environment correctly, and that relaxing his vigilance would be the mistake that finally killed him.

It was the appraisals that had formed around the accident, however, that gave his avoidance its particular shape. Viktor had come to believe that the world was fundamentally and irreversibly dangerous - not in the abstract way a risk-briefing describes danger, but in a visceral, cellular way that had dismantled everything he had previously understood about control, competence, and survival. His beliefs about his own mastery, about the reliability of machines and bodies, had been destroyed in those seconds of freefall. What frightened him most was the accompanying sense that he felt nothing - or rather, that what he felt was a kind of interior deadness, as though the man who had once loved flying had been incinerated along with the aircraft. These appraisals pressed him toward avoidance with a logic that felt unassailable: if the world was dangerous and his body an unreliable instrument, then any encounter with medical settings - hospitals, ambulances, even a routine physical examination - was an invitation to confirm the worst. He declined a mandatory flight medical, citing scheduling conflicts, and had not seen a physician since his discharge from acute care. He had also quietly given up the activities that had once anchored his off-duty life: long trail runs, weekend flying with civilian clubs, dinners with his wife's extended family. What remained was a stripped-down daily existence, and he had begun rigidly controlling his eating as one of the few domains where he felt any agency at all. Yet this withdrawal, over time, had not quieted the system - it had starved him of the corrective experiences that might have begun to loosen the threat appraisals, and the absence of normal life had itself become evidence that something was permanently wrong with him. The avoidance kept the triggers potent and the threat state elevated; the constricted life confirmed his belief that he was already, in some meaningful sense, dead inside.

Viktor sought help after his wife told him she no longer recognised him. He came to the first session guarded and precise, a man accustomed to debriefs rather than disclosures. What he most feared was that treatment would confirm the deadness was permanent. What he most hoped - though he offered this only at the end of the session, quietly - was that he might one day sit in a cockpit again and feel something other than terror.
